title: Ezekiel 20:27–44
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to speak to the house of Israel. He recounts that once in the land the fathers offered sacrifices on every high hill and under every thick tree; the LORD questions the high place where they went, and its name, Bamah, remained. The present generation, he says, still pollutes itself with idols and makes its sons pass through the fire, so he will not be inquired of by them. He rejects their thought of becoming like the nations who serve wood and stone and declares that with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out, he will be king over them (compare Exodus 6:6). He will gather them from the nations into the wilderness of the peoples, judge them face to face as he judged their fathers, make them pass under the rod, bring them into the bond of the covenant, and purge out the rebels. Then on his holy mountain all the house of Israel will serve him, he will accept them as a pleasant aroma and be sanctified among them before the nations, and they will remember their ways and loathe themselves. They will know that he is the LORD when he deals with them for his name’s sake and not according to their evil ways (compare 36:22, 31–32). Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat this promise of restoration, grounded in God’s name rather than Israel’s merit, as shared ground, while differing elsewhere on how renewal is applied to individuals.

verses.text: “Therefore, son of man, speak to the house of Israel, and tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Moreover, in this your fathers have blasphemed me, in that they have committed a trespass against me.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Ezekiel to speak of how the fathers blasphemed him by their trespass. Unfaithfulness continued in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the history moving from the wilderness to the land. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing a further stage of Israel’s rebellion.

verses.text: For when I had brought them into the land which I swore to give to them, then they saw every high hill and every thick tree, and they offered there their sacrifices, and there they presented the provocation of their offering. There they also made their pleasant aroma, and there they poured out their drink offerings.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people offering sacrifices on every high hill and under every thick tree. Worship became scattered and corrupt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the provocation of worship offered on the people’s own terms. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against worship shaped by human preference.

verses.text: Then I said to them, ‘What does the high place where you go mean?’ So its name is called Bamah to this day.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD questioning the high place where they went, a site that kept its name. The question exposes their error.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a wordplay on the name Bamah that marks the persistence of false worship. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a pointed rebuke.

verses.text: “Therefore tell the house of Israel, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Do you pollute yourselves in the way of your fathers? Do you play the prostitute after their abominations?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether the present generation pollutes itself in the way of its fathers. The past is repeated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the present generation implicated in the sins of the past. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to honest self-examination.

verses.text: When you offer your gifts, when you make your sons pass through the fire, do you pollute yourselves with all your idols to this day? Should I be inquired of by you, house of Israel? As I live, says the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD naming their idolatry, including making their sons pass through the fire, and refusing to be inquired of. Sin blocks fellowship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD returning to the elders’ inquiry of 20:3. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as explaining why God will not answer those who cling to idols.

verses.text: “ ‘ “That which comes into your mind will not be at all, in that you say, ‘We will be as the nations, as the families of the countries, to serve wood and stone.’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD rejecting the people’s wish to be like the nations, serving wood and stone. God will not let them go so easily.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God overruling the people’s plan to abandon their calling. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God’s purpose for Israel is not set aside by their wishes.

verses.text: As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “surely with a mighty hand, with an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out, I will be king over you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD declaring that with a mighty hand and outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out, he will be king over them. God remains their King.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see exodus language (compare Exodus 6:6) now joined with wrath. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as affirming God’s kingship over his people.

verses.text: I will bring you out from the peoples, and will gather you out of the countries in which you are scattered with a mighty hand, with an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD promising to gather the scattered people from the nations. A new exodus is coming, like the first one from Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign regathering of his people. Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s faithfulness beyond exile.

verses.text: I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD bringing them into the wilderness of the peoples to judge them face to face. Restoration involves confrontation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the wilderness as a place of judgment and renewal (compare Hosea 2:14). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of God’s purifying work.

verses.text: Just as I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he will judge them as he judged their fathers in the wilderness of Egypt. History provides the pattern.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see continuity in God’s dealings with each generation. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober reminder that God’s judgment is consistent.

verses.text: “I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD making them pass under the rod and bringing them into the bond of the covenant. The shepherd counts and claims his flock.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image of a shepherd examining the flock (compare Leviticus 27:32). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as God renewing his covenant claim.

verses.text: I will purge out from among you the rebels and those who disobey me. I will bring them out of the land where they live, but they shall not enter into the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD purging out the rebels so they will not enter the land. Not all who return will share the blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God separating within his people (compare 34:17). Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that restoration includes purification.

verses.text: “ ‘As for you, house of Israel, the Lord GOD says: “Go, everyone serve his idols, and hereafter also, if you will not listen to me; but you shall no more profane my holy name with your gifts and with your idols.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling the house of Israel to go serve their idols if they will not listen, but no longer profane his name. The choice is stark.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an ironic summons that exposes the people’s divided worship. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to end the profaning of God’s name.

verses.text: For in my holy mountain, in the mountain of the height of Israel,” says the Lord GOD, “there all the house of Israel, all of them, shall serve me in the land. There I will accept them, and there I will require your offerings and the first fruits of your offerings, with all your holy things.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the promise that on God’s holy mountain all the house of Israel will serve him and he will accept their offerings. Worship will be restored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God promising acceptable worship in the future. Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about the hope of restored communion.

verses.text: I will accept you as a pleasant aroma when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries in which you have been scattered. I will be sanctified in you in the sight of the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD accepting the people as a pleasant aroma and being sanctified in them before the nations. God’s holiness will be displayed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the people themselves as an offering pleasing to God (compare Ephesians 5:2). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God’s glory revealed in his people.

verses.text: You will know that I am the LORD when I bring you into the land of Israel, into the country which I swore to give to your fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people coming to know the LORD when he brings them into the land promised to their fathers. Knowledge of God grows through his faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to his oath to the fathers. Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God keeping his promises.

verses.text: There you will remember your ways, and all your deeds in which you have polluted yourselves. Then you will loathe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that you have committed.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people remembering their ways and loathing themselves for their evils. True repentance follows restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see repentance as the fruit of God’s gracious dealings (compare 36:31). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about godly sorrow.

verses.text: You will know that I am the LORD, when I have dealt with you for my name’s sake, not according to your evil ways, nor according to your corrupt doings, you house of Israel,” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD dealing with them for his name’s sake, not according to their evil ways. Grace, not merit, shapes the outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see salvation grounded in God’s name rather than human deeds (compare 36:22, 32). Both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s grace.
